I. 
INTRODUCTION 
During its 2024 session, the Maryland General Assembly enacted Senate Bill 959, 
the Distributed Renewable Integration and Vehicle Electrification (“DRIVE”) Act, 
codified in Md. Code Ann., Public Utilities Article (“PUA”), Title 7, Subtitle 10.1 The 
DRIVE Act required investor-owned electric companies (“Utilities”) to file with the 
Commission on or before July 1, 2025, proposals for a pilot program or temporary tariff 
for electric distribution system support services (“EDSSS”) as provided through virtual 
power plant (“VPP”) and/or vehicle-to-grid (“V2G”) programs, in addition to requirements 
for certain time-of-use (“TOU”) rate proposals and enhanced incentives for the installation 
of renewable on-site generating systems.2 
On July 11, 2024, the Commission issued Order No. 91218 for the purpose of 
implementing the DRIVE Act. The Commission directed the Utilities to file with the 
Commission on or before July 1, 2025, EDSSS proposals for a pilot program or temporary 
tariff, among other requirements.3 Subsequently, Baltimore Gas and Electric Company 
(“BGE”), Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco”) and Delmarva Power & Light 
Company (“Delmarva”) (together the “PHI Companies” or “PHI”, and together with BGE

II. 
BACKGROUND 
The EDSSS requirements in the DRIVE Act, as codified under PUA § 7-1005, 
mandate that the Utilities establish pilot programs or temporary tariffs to compensate 
owners and aggregators of distributed energy resources (“DERs”) for EDSSS. Each Utility 
was required to submit its program proposal(s) by July 1, 2025, for Commission approval. 
While municipal utilities and cooperative utilities may also establish such programs, the 
Utilities are restricted from enrolling renewable on-site generating systems with a 
cumulative nameplate capacity exceeding two percent of their highest recorded coincident 
peak demand. Furthermore, the Commission was authorized to require the Utilities to offer 
upfront incentives or rebates for the installation of these systems, provided customers enroll 
in an approved EDSSS program for at least five years. Special provisions allow for 
additional or prioritized incentives specifically for low- or moderate-income customers. 
PUA § 7-1006 addresses incentives for customers to install renewable on-site generating 
systems. Among other things, the Commission is required to consider setting incentive 
limits to balance deployment goals with customer impact and consult with the Maryland 
Energy Administration (“MEA”) to ensure coordination with other available State and 
federal incentives. PUA § 7-1007 addresses the cost recovery provisions for the Utilities 
participating in programs under the DRIVE Act. The companies are entitled to recover all 
reasonable costs associated with administering programs and offering upfront incentives

incentive mechanisms to cover expenses related to distributed energy resources or

THRESHOLD 
POLICY

IMPACTING

APPROVALS 
A. 
RELIEF Act Impacts on DRIVE Act Program Proposals 
On April 13, 2026, the Maryland General Assembly approved the Utility Reducing 
Energy Load Inflation for Everyday Families (“RELIEF”) Act,10 which was signed into 
law by Governor Moore on May 12, 2026. This legislation impacts the DRIVE Act. The 
RELIEF Act reduces ratepayer surcharges due to affordability concerns, while continuing 
to potentially fund these surcharges if any funds are available in the Maryland Strategic 
Energy Investment Fund (“SEIF”) administered by MEA. The RELIEF Act specifically 
modifies the DRIVE Act by changing PUA § 7-1007 to require that MEA now provide any 
DRIVE Act incentives, subject to available funding, in consultation with the Commission, 
whereas previously the Commission could approve electric company incentives in 
coordination with MEA. Also, PUA § 7-1008 was modified by the RELIEF Act to remove 
a section that allowed utility cost recovery for DRIVE Act incentives. Taken together, these 
changes mean the Utilities can no longer offer incentives for DRIVE Act participation and 
receive cost recovery. Instead, DRIVE Act incentives must be funded through MEA 
programs, to the extent any SEIF funds are available. 

10 Senate Bill 841/House Bill 1532. 

5 
Commission Decision 

The Commission interprets a payment for participating in a DRIVE Act program 
(such as $/kW-yr or $/kW-season) as a payment for providing a grid service in response to 
a utility dispatch order, not as an incentive. Locational adders provide grid service value 
and the Commission does not consider them an incentive payment. Conversely, the 
Commission considers an incentive to be direct or indirect compensation designed to 
promote participation in utility DRIVE Act program offerings by reducing cost barriers to 
entry. These interpretations will impact several of the utility DRIVE Act proposals. The 
Commission directs the Utilities to redirect their efforts to provide incentives by 
coordinating their funding needs with MEA. 
The Commission’s incentive determination will apply to Potomac Edison’s 
proposed Low-to-Moderate Income (“LMI”) Incentives, which cannot be funded through 
utility rates. Potomac Edison has also proposed a connectivity incentive of up to $150 per 
connected year to be paid annually upon the completion of a connectivity verification and 
test.11 Since this incentive is not performance based—i.e., it is not a payment for grid 
services—this incentive cannot be funded through utility rates. Potomac Edison also 
provides locational adders: $50 for residential Bring-Your-Own-Device (“BYOD”) 
batteries and electric vehicle (“EV”) chargers and 20 percent of the performance payment 
for aggregations.12 Therefore, these locational adders can be funded through utility rates. 
Although PHI was less specific, indicating that it plans to file a supplemental plan 
in 180 days to deploy behind-the-meter (“BTM”) battery energy storage systems (“BESS”) 

11 Potomac Edison Revised EDSSS Pilot at 9-10. 
12 See Potomac Edison Revised EDSSS Pilot, Appendix D.

at a cost of no more than $5 million to support incentives, rebates, and other mechanisms 
to increase participation from underserved communities, these incentives likely cannot be 
funded through utility rates if they are only used to increase customer participation. Finally, 
this determination also applies to BGE’s Medical Needs BESS proposal where BGE 
proposes to provide BGE-owned batteries at no cost to customer-site hosts to serve 300 
medical needs customers. BGE’s Medical Needs BESS program cannot be funded through 
utility rates because the customer participation is incentivized using a free battery. 
B. 
Integrating Demand Response EmPOWER Programs into DRIVE Act 
Pilot Programs 

BGE, PHI, and Potomac Edison generally support or propose moving various 
demand response programs, such as utility-owned direct load control (“DLC”) devices and 
smart thermostat offerings, to DRIVE Act programs, citing better alignment with the 
legislative intent for peak load reduction as EmPOWER shifts toward greenhouse gas 
abatement. They also argue that integration would improve efficiency, simplify program 
management by centralizing resources, and align demand response with the DRIVE Act’s 
intent as well as enable immediate pilot scaling. Conversely, SMECO opposes such a 
move, noting that the DRIVE Act does not currently apply to cooperatives while expressing 
concern over potential cost increases and program appropriateness.13 
Commission Technical Staff (“Staff”) does not oppose the transition of EmPOWER 
programs to the companies’ EDSSS pilot program framework, provided that metrics 
remain consistent and pilot performance does not duplicate existing program impacts.14 

13 Maillog No. 328618, SMECO Supplemental Comments at 1 (Apr. 1, 2016). 
14 Staff Comments at 10. 

7 
Staff recommends that PHI and BGE explicitly identify included EmPOWER elements to 
ensure reporting remains non-duplicative, asserting that demand-side programs should be 
funded exclusively by either the DRIVE Act or EmPOWER.15 
The Office of People’s Counsel (“OPC”) objects to integrating EmPOWER 
demand response into the DRIVE Act pilots, citing “core design defects.”16 OPC argues 
that shifting existing programs would prevent the accurate measurement of incremental 
performance and risk utility device ownership expansion and customer confusion, asserting 
that “a pilot should test new capabilities, not mainly repackage capabilities that already 
exist.”17 OPC could support the transition but only if EmPOWER cost recovery is 
maintained, and Utilities are barred from counting existing demand response toward new 
VPP targets.18 
MEA supports the Utilities consolidating their programs but recommends a process 
with stakeholder input.19 MEA emphasizes the need for separate reporting of new VPP 
resources versus legacy demand response to accurately measure the DRIVE Act pilots’ 
success.20 
Other stakeholder reactions to the proposed transition of EmPOWER demand 
response resources into DRIVE Act pilots are mixed. SUN, SEIA, and CHESSA oppose 
the move, arguing it deviates from the DRIVE Act’s intent to focus on battery dispatch 
with onsite renewables rather than re-packaging demand response.21 While Advanced

Commission Decision 

The Commission agrees with various stakeholder arguments that re-packaging 
existing EmPOWER demand response programs would prevent accurate assessment of 
incremental enrollment and performance, in addition to expanding utility ownership of 
devices. The Commission agrees with the Utilities that inclusion of demand response 
resources offers potential efficiencies and the orchestration of heterogeneous DERs, such 
as solar and energy storage and demand response, as a pilot learning. In Order No. 91917, 
the Commission stated a willingness to broaden the pilot’s scope to allow aggregator 
participation and demand reduction in VPPs. Specifically, the Commission stated that 
“expanded VPP programs should include aggregator participation where aggregators bring 
C&I participation and demand reduction resources in addition to residential solar, storage 
and bidirectional EVs.”24 The Commission did not intend for the integration or upgrading 
of existing EmPOWER demand response programs into DRIVE Act programs. Integration 
or upgrading of existing EmPOWER demand response programs is better reserved for 
future consideration of permanent VPP programs.

C. 
Net Energy Metering Compensation 
BGE proposes that net energy metering (“NEM”) customers receive reduced 
compensation (up to $150/kW per year versus up to $300/kW for non-NEM) and not 
receive performance payments for distribution energy resource aggregator (“DERA”)-
dispatched events.25 PHI states that NEM customers will be eligible to participate but may 
not be eligible to receive NEM credits during call events.26 Potomac Edison is silent on 
NEM compensation. 
Several organizations, including SUN, SEIA, CHESSA, CPower, and a coalition 
of companies (including GoodLeap, Tesla, and Enphase), oppose proposals that would 
reduce payment or compensation for NEM customers participating in the DRIVE Act 
pilots. They argue that reducing compensation is discriminatory (against NEM customers) 
and will harm enrollment, noting that NEM compensates for energy while performance 
payments compensate for capacity.27 SUN specifically requests that NEM customers 
receive bill credits for exported energy and the same performance payment as non-NEM 

25 BGE Revised EDSSS Pilot at 31 and 33. 
26 PHI Revised EDSSS Pilot at 18, n.19. 
27 Residential Industry Comments at 2. 

10 
customers.28 SEIA and CHESSA argue that export-capable NEM customers provide more 
valuable, dispatchable capacity than simple load reducers.29 CPower states that BGE 
should not be allowed to exclude NEM accounts from the Aggregator model.30 
Commission Decision 

The Commission is concerned that combining NEM with separate, additional 
compensation for peak load reduction can be considered double counting. Under NEM, 
exported energy offsets consumption at full retail rates. If that same export also participated 
in a performance-based program that pays for reducing load during a peak event, the 
devices would get paid twice for the same result, with no incremental net peak kW 
reduction benefit. However, this scenario might not be true all the time, so there may be 
some incremental net peak kW reduction benefit from NEM devices participating in events 
that support the local grid. 
Without prejudicing actions the Commission may take on this or other matters 
involving NEM compensation in the future, the Commission is persuaded that BGE’s NEM 
compensation proposal to halve NEM compensation for its BYOD pilot program is a good 
compromise proposal appropriate for a pilot program. BGE reasons that this approach “will 
provide NEM customers with a compelling incentive that offers an option between selling 
their production back to the grid or participating in events that support the local grid. We 
believe this approach maintains fairness and simplicity across the customer base.”31 
However, it is unclear why BGE did not apply the same rationale for NEM compensation

specificity, and Potomac Edison does not address NEM compensation at all. Therefore, the 
Commission directs all Utilities to propose adjustments to their NEM compensation for 
their DRIVE Act programs to consider partial compensation, but not full compensation. 
While BGE’s 50-percent compensation proposal is a good middle ground, Utilities may 
propose other amounts of partial compensation as this could be a valuable pilot learning to 
determine NEM customer responsiveness to partial compensation approaches. 
D. 
Bill Impacts 
BGE and Potomac Edison’s bill impacts are projected to be less than $1 monthly 
for residential customers.32 Excluding BGE’s Medical BESS and 2WDLC programs will 
reduce BGE’s megawatt (“MW”) impact by 26 percent and likely significantly reduce 
BGE’s customer bill impact. Excluding Potomac Edison’s ESR Thermostat Program 
transition from EmPOWER will also reduce Potomac Edison’s MW impact and likely its 
bill impact by approximately 35 percent. Eliminating the LMI customer enrollment bonus 
will also reduce Potomac Edison’s projected bill impact. 
PHI’s bill impacts are relatively high in both their recommended and alternative 
scenario proposals33 when compared to the BGE and Potomac Edison proposals. PHI’s 
recommended proposal for Large Non-Residential (“C&I”) class is 60 MWs of peak load 
reduction, and PHI’s alternative scenario proposal is 30 MWs peak load reduction. Pepco’s 
bill impact is a maximum of $3.50 per month in Year 3 for PHI’s recommended proposal 
of 60 MWs peak load reduction as compared to $2.94 per month in Year 3 for PHI’s

a maximum of $2.29 per month in Year 3 for PHI’s recommended proposal as compared 
to $2.04 per month in Year 3 for PHI’s alternative scenario proposal.35 However, by 
excluding EmPOWER programs from DRIVE Act pilots, this will reduce PHI’s MW

bill impact of removing EmPOWER programs is unknown on both the PHI recommended

Commission Decision 
In light of affordability concerns, the Commission will not approve PHI’s 
recommended proposal for a 60 MW Large Non-Residential C&I program but instead will 
approve PHI’s 30 MW alternative scenario proposal as a precaution, since the total bill 
impact of removing PHI’s EmPOWER programs is unknown. BGE, PHI and Potomac 
Edison are directed to file informational filings on new budget and bill impacts with the 
eliminated programs removed and NEM compensation considered to move these updated 
projections into the record. PHI may petition the Commission to reconsider its decision to 
deny PHI’s Large Non-Residential C&I proposal if the company can demonstrate a 
significantly lower bill impact.

V. 
COST RECOVERY AND RECONCILIATION 
A. 
Cost Recovery 
BGE requests approval to establish a DRIVE Act surcharge mechanism, which 
would include capital expenditures associated with the programs that should be recovered 
over the assets’ useful lives. BGE also requests a regulatory asset for non-capital costs that 
cannot be recovered in a single year, such as programming. The surcharge would be 
updated annually and include current year forecasted costs, return on capital, and a true-up 
for the prior period.50 PHI proposes to implement a surcharge to recover administrative and 
incentive costs. The revenue requirement recovered through the surcharge would include

B. 
Reconciliation 
OPC recommends a uniform surcharge reconciliation process and further argues 
that the Commission’s cost recovery and reconciliation framework must allow for 
meaningful review on a developed record, which cannot happen with a routine 
administrative meeting process. OPC therefore recommends a formal but more streamlined 
reconciliation process than a full base-rate-style case, such as a recurring annual hearing 
for purchased power or gas adjustment proceedings.57 
Staff proposes that the surcharge rate should be approved administratively, similar 
to STRIDE filings, in lieu of litigated proceedings, given the short pilot timeframe. All 
parties should be allowed to question the Utilities on cost recovery.58 Accordingly, Staff 
proposes the following reconciliation process and timeline:59 
1. Initial Surcharge: Reflective of Year 1 costs and takes effect after tariffs 
are approved; 
2. Year 2 Surcharge Filing: Utilities file 60 days prior to the 
commencement of Year 2 surcharge rates;

4. Surcharge Adjustment: Reconciliation activity to be reflected as an add-
on to the Year 2 surcharge rate after Commission review and approval; 
5. Year 2 Reconciliation/Program Evaluation: Final filing approximately 
90 days after Year 2 to fully reconcile collections, ensure complete cost 
recovery, and evaluate if the program should be permanent; and 
6. Long-Term Cost Recovery: If the program continues, Staff recommends

Commission Decision 
The Commission accepts Staff’s recommendation for a reconciliation process and 
timeline in the Administrative Docket, in which the Commission has substantial experience 
with gas and electric surcharge reconciliations. It has not been demonstrated that OPC’s 
recommendation for a litigated reconciliation proceeding offers substantial benefit over the 
less burdensome process recommended by Staff.

All the Utilities are using third parties for EM&V. Measurement may require

E. 
Interconnection 
BGE proposes that customers who wish to enroll devices that generate or store 
energy must submit an interconnection application. PHI states that NEM customers 
enrolling in DRIVE Act pilot programs will need to submit a new interconnection 
application for export, and customers with a BESS serving resiliency needs will need to 
submit an interconnection application for export and that V2G will be part of the pilot.

Many parties oppose utility requirements that NEM customers must submit a new 
interconnection application to participate, arguing new applications should only be 
required if the customer seeks to increase their export capacity for the pilot.78 
Commission Decision 
The Commission recently approved emergency regulations in RM94, which 
modified the definition of a minor equipment modification that governs the need for a new 
interconnection application. The Commission cannot predetermine here if an individual 
project meets the definition of a minor equipment modification. However, a Utility may be 
found to be non-compliant should a complaint arise involving the utility requiring an 
interconnection customer to submit a new interconnection application for project changes 
that are not minor equipment modifications pursuant to the COMAR 20.50.09.02 
definition. To that end, the Utilities should not place obstacles that require new 
interconnection applications or restudy for NEM customers as a broad policy prerequisite 
for VPP pilot program participation.

VII. 
CONCLUSION 
The Commission is generally pleased with the Utilities’ revised EDSSS pilot 
program proposals that are largely compliant with the scope of, and cure deficiencies 
identified in, Order No. 91917. Despite not all of the proposed programs being approved, 
the Utilities have all made meaningful revisions to their EDSSS pilot program proposals 
that will contribute measurably to the DRIVE Act’s objective for EDSSS programs with a 
cumulative nameplate capacity not exceeding two percent of their highest recorded 
coincident peak demand. The most recent Commission Ten-Year Plan85 contains forecasts 
for coincident peak demand gross of demand-side management (“DSM”) programs, 
including forecasts for 2025. Coincident peak load gross of DSM programs is an 
appropriate threshold for measuring statute compliance because EDSSS programs will 
have a netting impact on gross demand. Each Utility’s approved proposal complies with
